qs.q: A pathologist is examining an intestinal resection specimen from a patient with inflammatory bowel disease. The findings include transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone mucosal appearance affecting the terminal ileum. Which condition is most consistent with these morphological features?
qs.e: Crohn's disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance that can affect any part of the GI tract, most commonly the terminal ileum. Ulcerative colitis is restricted to the colon, is continuous, and involves mucosal inflammation only.

qs.q: Following a surgical resection of the terminal ileum, a patient is most at risk for a deficiency in which specific nutrient?
o: Deficiency in vitamin B twelve following ileal resection
Deficiency in folic acid following ileal resection
Deficiency in elemental iron following ileal resection
Deficiency in dietary carbohydrates following ileal resection
qs.e: Vitamin B12 and bile salts are absorbed in the ileum, so disease or resection of the terminal ileum leads to Vitamin B12 deficiency. Iron and carbohydrates are primarily absorbed earlier in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman undergoes resection of a segment of the terminal ileum and subsequently develops chronic watery stools. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism of diarrhea in this patient?
o: Accelerated transit reducing nutrient exposure time
Unabsorbed bile acids stimulating colonic secretion
Direct mucosal injury impairing sodium absorption
Excessive secretion driven by circulating hormones
qs.e: Inflammatory diarrhea results from direct damage to the intestinal mucosa, which interferes with the absorption of sodium salts and water. This is distinct from osmotic, secretory, or motility-related mechanisms.

qs.q: A patient undergoes surgical resection of the terminal ileum. Which digestive function is most likely impaired? ---
qs.e: The terminal ileum is the principal site for active bile-salt reabsorption. Resection therefore increases fecal bile-salt loss and disrupts enterohepatic recycling.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The ileum is the distal part of the small intestine, crucial for bile acid reabsorption and immune surveillance. Clinicians must recognize its role in malabsorption, Crohn’s disease, and surgical resections. Understanding its relations helps avoid iatrogenic injury.

sections.p: The ileum is the final segment of the small intestine, extending from the jejunoileal junction to the ileocecal valve. It is a key site for nutrient absorption and immune function.
It begins at the jejunoileal junction and ends at the ileocecal valve. The mucosa has villi and microvilli, and the submucosa contains lymphoid aggregates.
Adjacent structures include the cecum, appendix, and mesenteric vessels. The ileocecal valve separates it from the colon.
Supplied by the ileocolic artery (branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and drained by the ileocolic vein.

sections.p: Parasympathetic via vagus and pelvic splanchnic nerves; sympathetic via mesenteric plexus.
Absorbs bile acids, vitamin B12, and remaining nutrients. It also hosts immune cells that sample luminal antigens.
Common issues include Crohn’s disease, ischemia, and surgical resections. Complications can lead to malabsorption and strictures.
Remember the ileal brake: fat stimulates PYY release, slowing gastric emptying. In surgery, avoid damaging the ileocecal valve.

faq.q: Why is the ileum important for vitamin B12 absorption?
faq.a: Intrinsic factor–B12 complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors.
